big_idea: Tree diagrams sort by 3 attributes by branching at each step.
learning_intention: We are learning to sort by 3 attributes using tree diagrams.
student_learning_goal: I can sort by 3 attributes using a tree diagram.
success_criteria: I can BRANCH at each level.
I can place items at the right BRANCH.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Detective Dot and Tally — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.

minds_on.hook: Detective Dot: 3 attributes! RED or BLUE? SQUARE or CIRCLE? BIG or SMALL? Each is a BRANCH on the tree! Dot opens: 'Three levels, three rules — same rule on every BRANCH!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Detective Dot and Tally puppets. 'Friends — last year you sorted by 2 attributes with Venn and Carroll. Today we sort by 3 attributes with a TREE DIAGRAM.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write TREE DIAGRAM on chart. 'Tree diagram = a branching diagram. At each level we branch by ONE attribute.'

Demonstrate. Draw a tree on chart:
- Top node: All shapes
- Level 1: RED branch, BLUE branch (attribute 1 = colour)
- Level 2 (under each colour): SQUARE branch, CIRCLE branch (attribute 2 = shape)
- Level 3 (under each shape): BIG branch, SMALL branch (attribute 3 = size)

'Each leaf at the bottom is one combination: RED + SQUARE + BIG, RED + SQUARE + SMALL, etc. 8 combinations total!'

Place cards at correct leaves. 'A red big square goes here. A blue small circle goes there.'

More examples (Canadian flavour):
- Hockey players: home/away → forward/defence → captain/not. 8 categories.
- Pets: dog/cat → big/small → fluffy/short hair. 8 categories.
- Weather: warm/cold → sunny/cloudy → windy/calm. 8 categories.

'Detective Dot says — 3 attributes, 3 branch levels. 2^3 = 8 leaves possible.'

Non-example. 'Trying tree with 1 attribute? Use Venn. With 2? Use Carroll. With 3? TREE.'

'Today we sort 30 data cards by 3 attributes.'

steps.instruction: Whole group: build a class tree with 8 leaves.
Three stations. A: Build tree with 12 cards. B: Read existing tree, place 8 new cards. C: Make own 3-attribute tree.
Stretch at C: explain why 3 attributes give 8 leaves.
Discuss when tree vs Venn vs Carroll.
steps.teacher_prompt: Show: 1 attr = list, 2 attr = Venn/Carroll, 3 attr = tree.

steps.instruction: STRATEGY COMPARE: After Station C, two pairs share trees with DIFFERENT attribute orders (colour-shape-size vs size-shape-colour). Class compares: same data, different trees? Cite English (1993) — combinatorial problems often have multiple valid orderings.
steps.teacher_prompt: Dot: 'Same data, different ORDER, different TREES — but every leaf still names ONE thing.'

differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at C: explain power of 2.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Sentence frame: 'This card is ___ AND ___ AND ___.'
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Children form a human tree, branching by 3 attributes.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: picks 3 attributes; branches correctly; places cards at correct leaves.

discussion_prompts: How many leaves in a 3-attribute tree?
When is tree better than Venn?
Dot's preview: tomorrow Tally turns these branches into a FREQUENCY TABLE (Lesson 2 — D1.1). What attribute would make the rows? Columns?
consolidation.exit_routine: Detective Dot's branch refrain — 'Three levels, three rules — same rule on every BRANCH!' (3x). Each child writes one branch path of their tree.

assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 1 surfaces children who handle 3-attribute reasoning.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child mixes branches at SAME LEVEL — repairing the cross-branching trap at Grade 3
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On three-attribute sorting (sort tree), the trap is branch-mixing — child applies different attribute orders within branches. English (1993, 'Children's Strategies in Solving Two- and Three-Dimensional Combinatorial Problems') frames consistent branching as the gateway to systematic data classification. Without it, Lesson 2's frequency tables cannot ground.

Today: 3-attribute sort tree with consistent branching. Tomorrow Tally turns the branches into a FREQUENCY TABLE (Lesson 2 — D1.1). Lesson 3 bar graphs; Lesson 4 mean/mode; Lesson 5 capstones.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair at Station A. Left subtree branches: RED → SQUARE/CIRCLE. Right subtree branches: BLUE → BIG/SMALL. Mixed.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'Detective Dot says — at one LEVEL, every branch uses the SAME attribute.'

Guide. 'Level 1 was COLOUR. Level 2 should be SHAPE for ALL — left and right.'

Redraw. Both sides level 2 = SQUARE/CIRCLE. Then level 3 = SIZE for all.

Generlise. 'Detective Dot says — pick attributes BEFORE drawing. Each level = one attribute. Both sides match.'

If still mixed: provide a level-attribute card stack to refer to.
common_misconceptions: Each subtree is independent. (Repair: all branches at one level = same attribute.)
Tree branches randomly. (Repair: tree is structured.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child names 3 attributes but mixes branches: give level-attribute card ('Level 1 = colour, Level 2 = shape, Level 3 = size'); child re-sorts following the card.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child applies same attribute twice in tree: drill 'each LEVEL = ONE attribute' rule; child labels each level.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child sorts but cannot articulate: force 'this branch is BIG-RED-CIRCLE because Level 1 = ___, Level 2 = ___, Level 3 = ___'.

parts_outline.task: Place 8 items in a 3-attribute tree (colour x shape x size).
Read a tree, identify 4 specific items at leaves.
Make your own tree with 3 attributes for your toys.
